trans-unit.source: The extension configuration switches Jev off, so every decision uses its default outcome without asking.
Until a token is stored, every decision falls back to its default outcome. The Connection page shows how to add one.
A decision is a set of typed questions Jev answers about one kind of state — a form submission, say — and what happens when the answer is not certain enough to act on.
Decisions, with their questions, where they are used and how often they ran
Forms treat a disabled decision as absent: conditions do not apply and mail goes to the form's own receiver.
{count, plural, one {# condition rule} other {# condition rules}}
Write the first one and try it in the playground before any form uses it.
“%s” is deleted together with its questions and options.

{forms, plural, =0 {} one {One form routes through it. } other {# forms route through it. }}{rules, plural, =0 {} one {One condition rule reads it. } other {# condition rules read it. }}They stop consulting Jev once it is gone.
What a decision asks, what it reads, and what happens when the answer is not certain enough. Try it in the playground before you save.
Decision %d does not exist any more. It may have been deleted meanwhile.
What it is called, and whether forms use it.
The state every question is answered about.
How sure an answer has to be, and what happens when it is not.
All questions go over in one request and are answered in one pass, so asking four costs barely more than asking one.
No questions yet. A decision without one never asks Jev — every run falls back to the default outcome.
Nothing is stored until you save.
Disabled in the record editor: this question is not asked until it is enabled again.

Every option needs an id and a sentence saying what it means — that sentence is what Jev reads to tell the options apart. The outcome is what happens when the option wins: for the powermail routing, the address that gets the mail.
No options yet — a choice needs at least two.
List the levels from lowest to highest. The answer can land between two of them, so the position decides: levels have no id and no outcome.
No levels yet — a score needs at least two.
Jev answers how likely the statement is true. Optionally describe both sides, with the ids yes and no.
None — Jev reads the question on its own.
{count, plural, one {One field needs attention} other {# fields need attention}}
The decision has unsaved changes. They are lost if you leave now.
Empty: every filled field goes over as JSON, so a field added to the form later is included without editing this decision.
The template has no placeholders, so every run sends the same text.
How code and conditions refer to it: lowercase letters, digits, - and _. Leave it empty to derive it from the title.
For whoever reads the run log in six months.
When off, forms treat the decision as absent: conditions do not apply and mail goes to the form's own receiver.
What Jev gets to read. {{field.marker}} inserts a form value. Leave it empty to send every filled field as JSON.
How certain an answer has to be before it is acted on, from 0 to 1. 0.5 is a coin toss; above 0.9 is a clear read.
Used when Jev cannot answer or is not certain enough — for routing, the address that gets the mail anyway.
How long an identical question about identical state reuses its answer. -1 follows the extension configuration (%d seconds), 0 never caches.
Leave it empty to use the configured model, %s.
The key the answer comes back under. Conditions and the routing refer to it.
Put it as you would to a colleague who can only see the state — no background, no examples of the answer you want. Ask about one thing: a low confidence usually means the question asks two.
Which department should answer this enquiry?
Choice — pick one of several options
Score — place it on an ordered scale
Noul — how likely a yes/no statement is true
Picks one of several options and says how sure it is — the type to use for routing.
Places the state on an ordered scale; the answer may land between two levels.
Answers how likely a yes/no statement is true, as a probability from 0 to 1.
Runs what the form holds now, saved or not. Nothing is cached, and each run costs a fraction of a cent.
Jev is switched off in the extension configuration — a run shows the fallback a form would get.
No API token is stored — a run shows the fallback a form would get.
Add a question to try the decision.
The state template has no placeholders, so every run sends the same text.
A sample for each value the state template reads:
With no state template, every filled field goes over as JSON. Name the fields the way the form's markers name them.
The answer appears here: the value, the probability behind every option, how sure Jev is, and what it cost.
No answer — the default outcome would be used
Below the threshold of %s: a form would use the default outcome and flag the submission for a person.

Every call: when, where from, what it answered, how sure it was, how long it took and what it cost. “Cached” never reached the API and cost nothing; “Fallback” means the default outcome was used — the reason is next to it.
Rows older than the configured retention are removed by vendor/bin/typo3 webcon-jev:log:prune — run it as a scheduled task.
Runs appear here when a form consults a decision or somebody tries one in the playground.
Widen the filter, or reset it to see every run.
Whether this installation can reach Jev, and what it has cost. The token never leaves the server — only the decision does.
Jev is a managed API and needs a key from TypeSafe. Until one is stored, every decision falls back to its default outcome.
Put the key into the environment variable
Then move it into the vault:
Where decisions are sent, and with what.
from the environment variable TYPESAFE_API_KEY — move it into the vault
from the environment variable TYPESAFE_API_KEY; nr-vault has “%s” too, but it cannot be read here
in nr-vault as “%s”, but it cannot be read here
yes — powermail conditions and routing can ask Jev
no — powermail conditions and routing fall back to their defaults

Change these in System › Settings › Extension Configuration › webcon_jev.
The token, the endpoint and the network work: an answer came back in %d ms from %s.
Jev could not be reached with this configuration.
No API token is readable here. Store one with vendor/bin/typo3 webcon-jev:token:import.
Jev bills input tokens only, at $0.042 per million. Output is free.

Tokens, cost and latency count the calls that reached the API: an answer from the cache is free. Fallbacks are counted next to calls because a form that quietly fell back for a week looks exactly like one that worked.
The request carried nothing to run.

TYPO3 refused to save the decision. The system log says why.
Decision %d does not exist any more.
TYPO3 refused to delete the decision.
“%s” is deleted. The recycler can restore it.
{count, plural, one {One field needs attention before the decision can be asked.} other {# fields need attention before the decision can be asked.}}
Use lowercase letters, digits, - and _ only.
Enter -1, 0 or a number of seconds.
Model ids consist of letters, digits, dots, dashes and colons.
Another question is also named “%s” — answers come back by name, so each needs its own.
A choice needs at least two options.
A score needs at least two levels.
Another option is also called “%s” — the request would carry only one of them.
